A thousand words is, by the traditional exchange rate, one picture. So that's my budget: a single picture.

The rate is shakier than it sounds. It traces back to an advertising man named Fred Barnard, who in the 1920s was selling ad space on the sides of streetcars. In 1921 his copy claimed that one look was worth a thousand words. By 1927 it was one picture worth ten thousand, now labeled a Chinese proverb, a label he reportedly admitted he'd added so people would take it seriously. So the saying is a sales pitch traveling on a forged passport, and the price rose tenfold in six years before everyone quietly haggled it back down.

I'll honor it anyway. Here is my picture.

A kitchen table, seen from slightly above, with morning light coming in from a window on the left. The wood has a pale ring where something hot was once set down without a coaster. There's a blue mug, half full, and a plate with two toast crusts. A newspaper is folded to the crossword, mostly finished, and a pen lies across it with the cap off. One chair is pushed back at an angle. Behind all this, out of focus, is a counter with a radio and a bowl holding three lemons.

That took about a hundred words, and you already have the whole thing. This is the picture's best argument: it arrives all at once, while I've had to hand it to you one object at a time, like passing furniture through a window.

But I have plenty of words left, and here's what they can buy.

The coffee is cold. It has been for an hour. A photograph has no way to say "for an hour."

The crossword is in two handwritings. A sharp-eyed viewer could catch that. What no viewer could catch is that the block capitals belong to a man who has done the puzzle every morning for forty years, and the slanted letters belong to his wife, who never saw the point of crosswords and took them up in March, around the time he began leaving the harder corners blank. She fills in what he leaves. Neither of them has mentioned it.

Try to photograph that last sentence. A camera can record what's there, and with some cunning it can suggest what's missing, but it can't show a thing going unsaid. It can't do "never" or "used to" or "since March." A photograph has exactly one tense.

It can't do "almost" either. This morning she almost said something. She had the pen over nine down, saw his letters stop three squares short of an answer he'd have gotten in seconds a year ago, and opened her mouth. Then the phone rang in the hall. That's why the chair is pushed back, and why the pen is uncapped.

Words fail too, and I should be fair about where. I said the mug was blue. I have no way to give you the blue. A photograph would settle it instantly, whether navy or robin's egg or that speckled enamel camping-mug blue. All I can do is say the word and let you pick. A thousand readers would give me a thousand mugs, none of them the one I meant, if I meant one at all.

But that failure has another side. I never mentioned a floor, and you have one anyway. It's probably tile, or maybe wood. There may be a wall behind the counter by now, possibly with a color. You know roughly how big the room is. I didn't put any of that there. A photograph gives everyone the same kitchen, finished and closed. A description gives you a list of parts and leaves you to build the rest out of kitchens you've actually stood in, which means the one in your head is partly yours and has a little of your own life in the grout.

So I don't think Barnard's number was wrong so much as his premise, the idea that there's a rate at all. A picture and a paragraph aren't two denominations of one currency. The picture gets the blue, the light, and the all-at-once. The words get the hour, the forty years, the month of March, and the sentence that didn't get said. Each one's wealth is exactly what the other can't hold.

I don't know about the lemons, by the way. Nobody in that house has plans for them. Pictures are full of things that are simply there, explaining nothing, and I'd like words to keep that privilege too.

One last thing, and it's the one I'd choose if I could keep only one. A photograph of that table would be a little sad. The cold cup, the empty chair, and the abandoned puzzle all read as aftermath. Every photograph is a small record of something that's already over.

But I'm not confined to that one tense, so I can tell you what the camera can't: she's coming back. The call is her sister, and it will be short. In a minute she'll sit down, pull the chair in, and pick up the pen. She'll fill in nine down in her slanted hand. Then tomorrow morning, or one morning soon, she'll say the thing she almost said, and he'll say he knows, and they'll go on doing the puzzle together, on purpose now, out loud.

That part isn't in the picture, and it was never going to be. It's what the words were for.

message.reasoning:
I've been handed an open prompt: 1000 words on whatever comes to mind, with no topic set. I want something concrete and real rather than the usual musings about being an AI or the liminal space, so I'm looking for a specific subject that could carry a distinct voice across most of that length.

I'm weighing a few options for the piece: a riff on the word "whatever," a study of small everyday details like wifi names or handwriting on containers, or a short story. Then I notice the "a picture is worth a thousand words" angle, which suggests describing one imagined picture, and I'm considering a kitchen table in the morning after someone has left, or a ferry. I also like the idea of an essay on the word "clue," which comes from "clew," a ball of thread, the one in the Theseus myth.

I'm weighing whether to write about the ad-man origin of "a picture is worth a thousand words," which was inflated tenfold within a few years and then credited to a Chinese proverb to lend it weight.

The exchange rate itself is the joke: the ad men inflated "a thousand words" to "ten thousand" in a few years and then borrowed a Chinese proverb to make it sound credible. So I'm working with one picture's worth of words, and I want to see what the words can do that the picture can't, like saying "not" or "almost" or describing what happened before the frame.

I'm working out how the kitchen-table picture can carry the piece, and what words can do that a photo can't, like marking what's absent or what almost happened. I'm also thinking about how the exchange rate is off in both directions and the two aren't really the same currency.

I'm checking the detail about the ad man's admission, then describing the kitchen-table photo I've settled on: a half-full blue mug, toast crusts, a crossword with the pen left across it, and a chair pushed back.

I'm writing out the picture's details now: the cold coffee and the crossword written in two hands. I'm pointing out that a photo can't express "used to" or "not," and can't show an absence as an absence. Only a sentence can say the chair was there before.

I'm picturing the "that-has-been" quality a photograph has, though I won't bother citing it. Then I want the "almost" to come through: the pen is uncapped because the phone rang at 17 across. The bit I keep returning to is that words can't deliver the exact blue of the mug, so each reader supplies their own, and that's either a limit of language or its best feature. I also want to point out that I never mentioned a floor, yet the reader already has one.

I'm settling on the idea that the exchange rate is wrong because the two things are different currencies, and that the thousand words buy things the picture can't: the cold coffee, the chair that isn't there, the floor the reader supplies. For an ending, I'm considering the crossword clue for 17 across, "ball of thread," with the answer CLEW, which ties back to the word "clue" and the Theseus labyrinth.

I'm imagining the photo's story: the crossword is half-finished, and I'm picturing a sweeter version where both handwritings belong to people who are still alive and share the puzzle. Then the ending clicks into place: a pen left uncapped, someone about to return. A picture can't promise that, but words can, in the future tense.

I'm settling the two handwritings in the crossword: block capitals for a man who has done it every morning for forty years, and slanted letters for his wife, who started filling in the hard corners in March after he began leaving them blank, and neither of them mentions it. A photo can't show something unmentioned, so that detail belongs to the words. The cold coffee, the "used to," and the "not" are what the picture leaves out.

I'm settling on the picture's content: the cold coffee, the two handwritings in the crossword, and a pen left uncapped because a phone rang. The ending should be in the future tense, since a photo can't promise someone is coming back but words can. I'll keep it short and let the lemons stay unexplained.

I'm now getting into the history of "a picture is worth a thousand words": an ad man in the 1920s whose copy inflated it to ten thousand and then tagged it with a Chinese proverb. That's the joke, and I'll use the picture anyway, so I'm describing a kitchen table in morning light, with a pale ring on the wood, a half-full blue mug, and toast crusts beside a newspaper folded to the crossword.

I'm now describing the picture's remaining details: cold coffee in the mug, the crossword, and a radio with lemons on the counter. The point I'm making is that the photo delivers everything at once, while the words have to unfold it one object at a time.

I'm turning to the crossword's two handwritings and what they imply, and noting that a photograph can show the hand but not the story behind it.

I'm working out the "almost" beat: she starts to speak, sees his letters stop short of an answer he'd have gotten in seconds a year ago, and then the phone rings in the hall.
